keyVerseText: I will shew thee, hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare;
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb חָוָה (châvâh) is a primitive root closely related to חֲוָא and חָיָה, suggesting a fundamental concept of life or living. Beyond the common English gloss of 'show' or 'declare,' its root sense encompasses the idea of making something alive or bringing it into expression, intensifying the act of revealing or declaring. This etymological background enriches the understanding of the word as not merely communicating information but vivifying truth through declaration.
usageInScripture: This verb appears six times in Scripture, consistently translated with nuances of 'show,' 'declare,' or 'shew,' emphasizing the act of making known or revealing. The top translations such as 'I will shew,' 'and I will shew,' and 'sheweth' indicate a strong focus on the intentional communication of knowledge or truth. The word's usage in various forms highlights its role in personal declaration and divine revelation, underscoring a dynamic process of making known what is otherwise hidden.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חָוָה as a verb that means to declare or make known is vital for grasping how God reveals Himself and His truth to humanity. It points to the active nature of divine communication, where God does not merely exist in silence but speaks life and truth into human experience. For the Christian faith, this underscores the importance of God’s self-disclosure through Scripture and ultimately in Christ, who is the living Word. The verb’s association with life further deepens the theological conviction that true revelation brings spiritual vitality and understanding.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 15:17, the speaker says, 'I will shew thee, hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare,' highlighting the verb חָוָה as central to the act of communicating witnessed truth. Here, 'I will shew' conveys a confident intention to reveal insight gained through experience, inviting attentive hearing. The use of this word enriches the verse by emphasizing the personal and deliberate nature of the revelation, underscoring the responsibility and privilege of declaring what God has made known.
